Bounds on sentence effects under monotone response and selection

Source: R/mtrbnd.R
mtrbnd.Rd

Asks what can be said about the effect of a harsher sentence (a longer term, custody against probation) on an outcome such as reconviction when who received which sentence was not random. With no assumption the mean outcome everyone would have under sentence t is known only to an interval (see sntbnd() for two sentences). Manski and Pepper (2000) narrow it with two assumptions about ordered treatments:

Usage

mtrbnd(y, z, ylo = 0, yhi = 1, assume = "both", w = NULL)

Arguments

y

The outcome of each person: numbers between ylo and yhi (0 or 1 for reconviction).

z

The sentence of each person: labels in their order of severity (a factor's levels, or the sorted values), two at least.

ylo, yhi

The least and the greatest possible outcome: one number each, ylo below yhi.

assume

"none", "mtr", "mts" or "both".

w

NULL for equal weights, or one weight from 0 per person.

Value

An object of class mtrbnd, a list: bnd, one row per sentence (z, share, mean, lower and upper of the mean outcome under it, and atelo, atehi, the bounds on its effect against the first sentence, NA for that one); assume; and range.

Details

  • monotone treatment response (MTR): each person's outcome does not fall as the sentence gets harsher (code y so that this holds); then those who got a milder sentence u < t would have at least their observed outcome under t, and those who got a harsher one at most theirs;

  • monotone treatment selection (MTS): those who received harsher sentences would, on average, have had outcomes at least as high under any one sentence (the courts sentence higher-risk people more harshly).

With P(u) the share and m(u) the mean outcome of those who received sentence u, and outcomes between ylo and yhi, the bound on the mean under t is, under MTR, from sum_{u <= t} m(u) P(u) + ylo P(z > t) to yhi P(z < t) + sum_{u >= t} m(u) P(u); under MTS, from ylo P(z < t) + m(t) P(z >= t) to m(t) P(z <= t) + yhi P(z > t); and under both, from sum_{u < t} m(u) P(u) + m(t) P(z >= t) to m(t) P(z <= t) + sum_{u > t} m(u) P(u) (their Proposition 2). The effect of t against the first (mildest) sentence is bounded by the difference of the bounds, its lower end at least 0 under MTR; these differences contain the effect but need not be its sharpest bounds.

References

Manski, C. F. and Pepper, J. V. (2000). Monotone instrumental variables: with an application to the returns to schooling. Econometrica, 68(4), 997-1010. doi:10.1111/1468-0262.00144

Examples

set.seed(13)
z <- factor(sample(c("fine", "probation", "custody"), 800, TRUE),
            levels = c("fine", "probation", "custody"))
y <- rbinom(800, 1, c(0.2, 0.35, 0.5)[as.integer(z)])
mtrbnd(y, z, assume = "both")
#> mtrbnd: bounds under both
#>          z   share      mean     lower     upper atelo     atehi
#>       fine 0.33750 0.2111111 0.2111111 0.3487500    NA        NA
#>  probation 0.33625 0.3680297 0.3150697 0.4017100     0 0.1905989
#>    custody 0.32625 0.4712644 0.3487500 0.4712644     0 0.2601533
mtrbnd(y, z, assume = "none")
#> mtrbnd: bounds under none
#>          z   share      mean   lower   upper atelo   atehi
#>       fine 0.33750 0.2111111 0.07125 0.73375    NA      NA
#>  probation 0.33625 0.3680297 0.12375 0.78750 -0.61 0.71625
#>    custody 0.32625 0.4712644 0.15375 0.82750 -0.58 0.75625
